nameStory: The butterfly bush earned its common name for good reason – its fragrant flower clusters are absolute magnets for butterflies! The scientific name honors two men: the genus Buddleja was named after English botanist Reverend Adam Buddle, while davidii commemorates French missionary Father Armand David, who was the first European to document this Chinese native in the 1800s.
description: Butterfly bush is a fast-growing deciduous shrub that can reach 6-12 feet tall and wide, creating an arching, fountain-like shape. It's covered in long, narrow leaves and produces dense, cone-shaped clusters of tiny, tubular flowers from summer into fall. Originally from China, this popular garden plant has escaped cultivation and now grows wild throughout New England. The flowers come in shades of purple, pink, white, or yellow and release a sweet, honey-like fragrance that's especially strong on warm days.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, cone-shaped clusters 4-10 inches long packed with tiny tubular flowers that have four petals and a small orange or yellow center 'eye'. The clusters feel papery and emit a sweet, honey-like fragrance that carries on the breeze.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves 4-10 inches long arranged in opposite pairs along the stems. They're dark green on top with a fuzzy, grayish-white underside that feels soft and woolly to the touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Fast-growing shrub with long, arching branches that create a graceful fountain shape. Stems are square in cross-section and feel slightly ridged when you run your finger along them.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry capsules that split open to release tiny seeds with papery wings. The spent flower clusters turn brown and papery, persisting into winter.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Older stems develop fibrous, shredding bark that peels away in strips, revealing lighter wood underneath. Young stems are smooth and green to reddish-brown.

habitat: Butterfly bush thrives in sunny, well-drained locations and is commonly found along roadsides, abandoned lots, railroad tracks, and forest edges. It tolerates poor soils and drought once established, making it successful in disturbed areas. You'll often spot it near old homesteads or escaped from gardens into nearby wild areas.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge late in spring, unfurling to show their distinctive woolly white undersides. The shrub leafs out later than many native plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season begins in mid-summer with fragrant flower clusters that attract clouds of butterflies and other pollinators. Dead-heading spent blooms encourages more flowers.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming until hard frost, with flower clusters gradually turning brown and papery. Leaves may yellow slightly before dropping, but fall color is unremarkable.
seasonality.winter: Bare stems show the characteristic square cross-section and fibrous, peeling bark. Brown, papery seed clusters often persist, rattling in winter winds.

funFact: A single butterfly bush can produce up to 3 million seeds per year, and each tiny seed can travel up to 100 miles on the wind – which explains how this Chinese native has managed to spread so widely from gardens into wild spaces across New England!
confusionNotes: Butterfly bush is sometimes confused with lilacs when not in bloom, but lilac leaves are heart-shaped and smooth on both sides, while butterfly bush leaves are lance-shaped with fuzzy white undersides. The square stems of butterfly bush are also a dead giveaway – lilac stems are round.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its popularity with gardeners and butterflies, butterfly bush is considered invasive in many areas because it crowds out native plants that provide better long-term habitat for wildlife. Many states now recommend native alternatives like New Jersey tea or ninebark for butterfly gardens.
compareHints: Butterfly bush is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England, but within the figwort family, it's most similar to verbascum (mullein). However, mulleins are typically biennials with thick, woolly leaves in a basal rosette and tall spikes of yellow flowers, while butterfly bush is a woody shrub with opposite leaves and cone-shaped flower clusters.
